deck.title: VPC — Virtual Private Cloud
deck.analogy: A VPC is your own plot of land in a huge city: you set the street layout (IP ranges), build rooms (subnets), choose which have doors to the street, and hire guards (security groups and NACLs).

subtopics.title: Public vs private: it's all about the route

Connecting VPCs: three very different tools

cards.front: What is an Amazon VPC?

back.answer: Your own private, fenced-off network in AWS; nothing gets in or out unless you build a door.
back.explanation: You choose IP ranges, subnets, internet access, and guards (SGs and NACLs).
back.mnemonic: A plot of land in a big city.

cards.front: In a VPC, what scope does a VPC have versus a subnet?

back.answer: A VPC lives in ONE region; a subnet lives in ONE Availability Zone.
back.explanation: So multi-AZ designs need multiple subnets.

cards.front: What do VPC route tables do?

back.answer: Each subnet's route table says 'traffic for X goes via Y'; they are the road signs.
back.explanation: Change the routes and you change the network.

cards.front: What is the VPC Internet Gateway (IGW)?

back.answer: The VPC's two-way front door: traffic can go out and the internet can come in to public IPs.

cards.sourceHeading: Public vs private: it's all about the route

cards.front: What makes a VPC subnet public?

back.answer: Its route table has a route to the IGW (0.0.0.0/0 → igw-xxx). No IGW route = private.
back.explanation: Not the name or the IPs, only the route.

cards.sourceHeading: Public vs private: it's all about the route

cards.front: What does a VPC NAT Gateway allow?

back.answer: Private instances can initiate outbound to the internet; the internet can never initiate inbound.
back.explanation: It swaps the return address and remembers who asked, so replies are routed back.
back.mnemonic: A receptionist who mails letters for everyone and bins unsolicited incoming mail.

cards.sourceHeading: Public vs private: it's all about the route

cards.front: Where does a NAT Gateway live and how do private subnets use it?

back.answer: In a public subnet; private subnets route 0.0.0.0/0 → nat-xxx.
back.explanation: It needs the IGW route itself to reach the internet.

cards.sourceHeading: Public vs private: it's all about the route

cards.front: Trap: one NAT Gateway shared by all AZs in a VPC. What's wrong?

back.answer: It's a hidden single point of failure; deploy one NAT Gateway per AZ with each private subnet routing to its local one.
back.explanation: If its AZ dies, every private subnet loses internet.

cards.sourceHeading: Public vs private: it's all about the route
cards.examTip: make NAT HA → one per AZ

cards.front: What are the characteristics of a VPC NAT Gateway (management, scaling, SGs, cost)?

back.answer: Managed, auto-scales (~45–100 Gbps), no security groups, pay per hour plus per GB.

cards.sourceHeading: Public vs private: it's all about the route

cards.front: NAT Instance vs NAT Gateway in a VPC: management and security groups?

back.answer: NAT instance is a legacy DIY EC2: you manage, patch and size it, and it can have an SG. The gateway is managed with no SG.

cards.sourceHeading: Public vs private: it's all about the route

cards.front: A NAT instance in a VPC isn't forwarding traffic. What must you do?

back.answer: Disable the source/destination check on the instance.
back.explanation: EC2 drops traffic not addressed to itself; a NAT forwards others' traffic.

cards.sourceHeading: Public vs private: it's all about the route

cards.front: How do IPv6 instances in a VPC get outbound-only internet access?

back.answer: Egress-only Internet Gateway; IPv6 has no NAT because every IPv6 address is public.

cards.sourceHeading: Public vs private: it's all about the route

cards.front: What does CIDR 10.0.0.0/16 mean, and how many addresses do /16 and /24 give?

back.answer: The first 16 bits are fixed; /16 ≈ 65,536 addresses, /24 = 256.

cards.front: What is the allowed VPC CIDR size range?

back.answer: /16 (largest) to /28 (smallest).

cards.front: How many IPs does AWS reserve in every VPC subnet?

back.answer: 5 (network, router, DNS, future, broadcast); a /24 gives 251 usable.

cards.front: What is the VPC no-overlap rule?

back.answer: VPCs you connect (peering, TGW, VPN to on-prem) must have non-overlapping CIDRs.
back.explanation: You can't peer 10.0.0.0/16 with 10.0.0.0/16, so plan ranges up front.

cards.front: Security Group vs NACL: what does each guard?

back.answer: SG guards the instance (its network interface); NACL guards the subnet boundary.

cards.sourceHeading: The two guards: Security Groups vs NACLs

cards.front: Security Group vs NACL: stateful or stateless?

back.answer: SG is stateful (remembers); NACL is stateless (no memory).
back.mnemonic: Receptionist with memory vs gate guard with none.

cards.sourceHeading: The two guards: Security Groups vs NACLs

cards.front: Security Group vs NACL: which rule types are supported?

back.answer: SG: allow only (default deny). NACL: allow and DENY.

cards.sourceHeading: The two guards: Security Groups vs NACLs

cards.front: Security Group vs NACL: how are rules evaluated?

back.answer: SG: all rules evaluated together. NACL: numbered, lowest first, first match wins.

cards.sourceHeading: The two guards: Security Groups vs NACLs

cards.front: Security Group vs NACL: what can rules reference?

back.answer: SG rules can reference other SGs; NACL rules only CIDR blocks.

cards.sourceHeading: The two guards: Security Groups vs NACLs

cards.front: Why do you never write return-traffic rules in a Security Group?

back.answer: SGs are stateful: if a request was allowed out, the reply is automatically allowed back in.

cards.sourceHeading: The two guards: Security Groups vs NACLs

cards.front: Trap: requests go out of the subnet but responses never return. Cause?

back.answer: The NACL is missing the ephemeral-port (1024–65535) outbound rule.
back.explanation: NACLs are stateless; replies need their own explicit rule on ephemeral ports.

cards.sourceHeading: The two guards: Security Groups vs NACLs

cards.front: How do you let only app servers reach the database using Security Groups?

back.answer: DB SG allows inbound (e.g. port 3306) from the app tier's security group (SG referencing).
back.explanation: It survives IP changes.

cards.sourceHeading: The two guards: Security Groups vs NACLs

cards.front: Trap: block traffic from a specific malicious IP in a VPC. What do you use?

back.answer: A NACL DENY rule; security groups have no deny.

cards.sourceHeading: The two guards: Security Groups vs NACLs

cards.front: Gateway vs Interface VPC Endpoint: which services?

back.answer: Gateway: S3 and DynamoDB only. Interface (PrivateLink): nearly any AWS service plus SaaS.

cards.sourceHeading: VPC Endpoints — private hallways to AWS services

cards.front: Gateway vs Interface VPC Endpoint: cost?

back.answer: Gateway is free; Interface is paid (per hour + per GB).

cards.sourceHeading: VPC Endpoints — private hallways to AWS services

cards.front: Gateway vs Interface VPC Endpoint: how do they work?

back.answer: Gateway is a route-table entry; Interface is an ENI (private network card) in your subnet.

cards.sourceHeading: VPC Endpoints — private hallways to AWS services

cards.front: Gateway vs Interface VPC Endpoint: reachability from peered VPCs or on-prem?

back.answer: Gateway is VPC-local only; Interface is reachable over peering, Transit Gateway, and VPN.

cards.sourceHeading: VPC Endpoints — private hallways to AWS services

cards.front: Private EC2 needs S3 access, cheapest and most secure. What do you use?

back.answer: A Gateway Endpoint, not a NAT Gateway.
back.explanation: NAT charges per GB; Gateway Endpoints are free.

cards.sourceHeading: VPC Endpoints — private hallways to AWS services

cards.front: What is the centralized endpoints pattern, and what is the S3 interface endpoint for?

back.answer: Interface Endpoints in one shared VPC serve many VPCs; the S3 interface endpoint serves on-prem private S3 access.
back.explanation: The Gateway endpoint can't be reached from on-prem.

cards.sourceHeading: VPC Endpoints — private hallways to AWS services

cards.front: What is VPC Peering?

back.answer: A direct private 1:1 link between exactly two VPCs; cross-account and cross-region work.

cards.sourceHeading: Connecting VPCs: three very different tools

cards.front: Trap: VPC A peers with B and B peers with C. Can A reach C?

back.answer: No — peering is NOT transitive; every pair needs its own peering plus route-table entries.

cards.sourceHeading: Connecting VPCs: three very different tools

cards.front: How many peering connections for a full mesh of n VPCs?

back.explanation: This is why peering suits only 2–3 VPCs.

cards.sourceHeading: Connecting VPCs: three very different tools

cards.front: VPC Peering: cost and CIDR constraints?

back.answer: Free to create (pay data transfer); no CIDR overlap allowed.

cards.sourceHeading: Connecting VPCs: three very different tools

cards.front: What is a Transit Gateway (TGW)?

back.answer: A regional hub-and-spoke router: attach VPCs, Site-to-Site VPNs and Direct Connect; all communicate transitively.
back.explanation: One attachment per VPC instead of a mesh.

cards.sourceHeading: Connecting VPCs: three very different tools

cards.front: How do you share a Transit Gateway cross-account and across regions?

back.answer: Share with AWS RAM; peer TGWs across regions.

cards.sourceHeading: Connecting VPCs: three very different tools

cards.front: Which AWS networking service supports multicast?

back.answer: Transit Gateway — the only AWS service supporting multicast.

cards.sourceHeading: Connecting VPCs: three very different tools

cards.front: How do you segment prod from dev VPCs on a Transit Gateway?

back.answer: Use per-attachment route tables so prod VPCs can't reach dev VPCs even though both attach to the hub.

cards.sourceHeading: Connecting VPCs: three very different tools

cards.front: How does PrivateLink expose a service?

back.answer: Provider puts an NLB in front and creates an endpoint service; consumers create an interface endpoint to reach that one service only.
back.explanation: It's one-direction, a service window, not a network merge.
back.mnemonic: A service window, not a network marriage.

cards.sourceHeading: Connecting VPCs: three very different tools

cards.front: PrivateLink and CIDR overlap / scale?

back.answer: Overlapping CIDRs are fine; scales to thousands of consumer VPCs without route-table sprawl.
back.explanation: There's no routing between networks, just an ENI.

cards.sourceHeading: Connecting VPCs: three very different tools

cards.front: Peering vs TGW vs PrivateLink: which to pick?

back.answer: 2–3 VPCs, full access → Peering. Many VPCs + VPN/DX, transitive → TGW. One service, overlapping CIDRs → PrivateLink.

cards.sourceHeading: Connecting VPCs: three very different tools

cards.front: What do VPC Flow Logs capture and where do they go?

back.answer: Traffic metadata (IPs, port, protocol, ACCEPT/REJECT) to CloudWatch Logs or S3; not packet contents.
back.explanation: Look for REJECTs to find SG/NACL blocks.

cards.front: VPC Flow Logs vs Traffic Mirroring?

back.answer: Flow Logs record metadata; Traffic Mirroring copies full packets to an inspection appliance.

cards.front: What is a bastion host and what is its SG chain?

back.answer: A DIY EC2 jump box in a public subnet; its SG allows 22 from your corporate IP, private instances allow 22 from the bastion's SG.
back.explanation: You build, patch, and guard it.

cards.front: Most secure way to administer private instances: bastion or SSM Session Manager?

back.answer: SSM Session Manager: no port 22, no public IP, no bastion, every session logged.
back.explanation: Sessions are logged to CloudTrail/S3.

cards.front: What is VPC Sharing via RAM?

back.answer: One account owns the VPC and other accounts launch resources into its subnets: many accounts, one network, no peering.

cards.front: Block all traffic from a specific IP address to your VPC resources.

back.answer: NACL deny rule.
back.explanation: Security groups can't deny.

choices.text: Route table blackhole on the IGW
choices.why: Not the mechanism for blocking an IP.

cards.front: Only the app tier may connect to the database.

back.answer: DB security group allows inbound from the app tier's SG.

choices.text: NACL allowing the app subnet CIDR
choices.why: Less elegant; breaks on IP changes.

choices.text: Public IP allow-list on the DB
DB SG allows inbound from the app SG

cards.front: Private EC2 must access S3 privately at the lowest cost.

back.answer: Gateway VPC Endpoint.
back.explanation: It's free; NAT Gateway is the expensive decoy.

choices.why: Charges per GB and goes via the internet.

cards.front: 25 VPCs plus on-premises via VPN must all communicate.

back.answer: Transit Gateway.
back.explanation: A peering mesh would be 300 connections.

choices.why: Hub for VPCs and VPN, transitive.

cards.front: Expose one application to a partner VPC; CIDR ranges overlap.

back.answer: PrivateLink (NLB + endpoint service).
back.explanation: Overlap doesn't matter.

cards.front: Single NAT Gateway: make the design highly available.

back.answer: One NAT Gateway per AZ, each private subnet routing to its local one.

choices.text: Two NATs in the same AZ

choices.why: Still a single point of failure.

cards.front: Private instances need to download OS updates.

back.answer: NAT Gateway in the public subnet plus private route 0.0.0.0/0 → NAT.

choices.text: NAT Gateway in the public subnet with a private default route
Put an IGW route in the private subnet
NAT Gateway in the private subnet

cards.front: Most secure way for admins to access private instances.

back.answer: SSM Session Manager.
back.explanation: No port 22, no bastion, fully logged.

cards.front: Determine why traffic to an instance is being rejected.

back.answer: VPC Flow Logs.
back.explanation: Metadata shows ACCEPT/REJECT; full packets need Traffic Mirroring.

cards.front: IPv6-only instances need outbound internet, no inbound.

back.answer: Egress-only Internet Gateway.
back.explanation: IPv6's NAT equivalent.

cards.front: A NAT instance stopped forwarding traffic.

back.answer: Disable the source/destination check.

cards.front: Outbound requests succeed but responses never arrive.

back.answer: NACL missing outbound ephemeral-port (1024–65535) rule.
back.explanation: NACLs are stateless.

choices.why: Requests succeed, so the path exists.
